v: Then one possessed by a demon, blind and mute, was brought to him and he healed him, so that the blind and mute man both spoke and saw.
All the multitudes were amazed, and said, “Can this be the son of David?”
But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, “This man does not cast out demons, except by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons.”
Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand.
If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand?
If I by Beelzebul cast out demons, by whom do your children cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
But if I by the Spirit of God cast out demons, then God’s Kingdom has come upon you.
Or how can one enter into the house of the strong man, and plunder his goods, unless he first bind the strong man? Then he will plunder his house.
“He who is not with me is against me, and he who doesn’t gather with me, scatters.
Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven men.
Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age, nor in that which is to come.
b: This passage records the miracle in which Jesus heals a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute, so that he could see and speak again. The miracle amazes the crowds, and some begin to ask whether he might be the Messiah. The Pharisees, however, react very negatively and accuse Jesus of driving out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. Jesus answers with powerful illustrations: if he casts out demons by the prince of demons, then Satan's kingdom is divided against itself and will fall. If he casts them out by the Spirit of God, then the Kingdom of God has come to them. Jesus adds the picture of entering a strong man's house to plunder his goods: one must first bind the strong man (here, Satan), implying that Jesus has authority to overcome evil spirits. Finally, Jesus speaks of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit as an unforgivable sin, stressing the deity and holiness of the Spirit.

Through this passage God teaches us to recognize Jesus' authority and deity. Jesus' actions not only show God's great power but also challenge how we understand and respond to God. God wants us to recognize and reject false accusations and to understand rightly God's work, especially the work of the Holy Spirit. Blasphemy against the Spirit, that is, refusing to acknowledge and accept what God plainly does through the Holy Spirit, is a grave sin, because at its root it rejects the truth and grace that come from God.
q: How do I view the Holy Spirit's work in my life? Have I ever ignored or misunderstood what the Spirit is doing? In the future, how can I become more sensitive and responsive to the Spirit's leading, so that I can experience God's work and blessing more fully?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you for showing your love and authority through the miracles of Jesus Christ. Help us stand firm on your truth when we face doubt and misunderstanding. Give us a discerning heart, so that we may honor and revere the work of your Holy Spirit. Do not let us be shaken by the prejudices and misunderstandings of the world, but help us keep walking in your love and truth. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Either make the tree good, and its fruit good, or make the tree corrupt, and its fruit corrupt; for the tree is known by its fruit.
You offspring of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.
The good man out of his good treasure brings out good things, and the evil man out of his evil treasure brings out evil things.
I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment.
For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”
b: In this passage Jesus teaches about the connection between our inner nature and our outward conduct. Using the picture of a tree and its fruit, he shows that a person's words and deeds are the natural expression of the condition of the heart. A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot bear good fruit. Applied to moral and spiritual life, this means that a person's words and actions reveal the good or evil within. Jesus calls his hearers a “brood of vipers,” rebuking those who appear to do good while being evil at heart. He stresses that a person's words show the state of the heart, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. Finally, Jesus warns that on the day of judgment everyone will be judged by their words, which will reveal their true nature and moral condition.

This passage shows us that words are not merely a tool of communication; they also reflect our spiritual and moral condition. Through Jesus' words God teaches us to examine whether our words and deeds agree, and whether they reflect a heart filled and renewed by God's Spirit. It is a reminder to hold to honesty and integrity, and to take responsibility for what we say and do. Our words have the power to bring life or death, so we should choose each one carefully, making sure it is constructive and honors God.
q: How do my words and actions show my faith? In the past week, were there moments when my words may have expressed a wrong attitude or feeling? How will I improve, so that I better reflect my faith and the goodness stored in my heart?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us through your word that our words and actions reflect the condition of our hearts. Help us to be watchful, so that our speech is full of love, kindness and truth, and so honors your name. Give us wisdom and strength to be more responsible in what we say, and to measure our conduct by the standard of Christ. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Then certain of the scribes and Pharisees answered, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from you.”
But he answered them, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks after a sign, but no sign will be given to it but the sign of Jonah the prophet.
For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the whale, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
The men of Nineveh will stand up in the judgment with this generation, and will condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, someone greater than Jonah is here.

The Queen of the South will rise up in the judgment with this generation, and will condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, someone greater than Solomon is here.
b: This passage describes the scribes and Pharisees demanding a sign from Jesus. Jesus condemns them as an evil generation and tells them that no sign will be given to them except the sign of Jonah. The sign of Jonah refers to Jesus' own death and resurrection: just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so Jesus will spend three days in the grave. Jesus also cites the men of Nineveh and the Queen of the South, who will stand up at the judgment and condemn this generation, because they listened to God's message and repented, while the people of the present day failed to recognize the greatness of Jesus.

Through this passage God reminds us that true faith is not based merely on seeing miracles, but on trusting God's word and deeply understanding what God does. Jesus stresses that his death and resurrection are the greatest sign, the ultimate display of God's power. The passage also teaches us to follow the repentance of the Ninevites and the Queen of the South, who listened to God's message and changed. It is a strong call to repent and rely wholeheartedly on Jesus, recognizing that he is greater than all the prophets and kings.
q: On my journey of faith, how do I respond to miracles? Do I look for physical proof to confirm my faith, or am I ready to experience God's presence through understanding Scripture and inner change? How can I make my life of faith deeper and more meaningful?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us, through Jesus Christ, the greatest sign of all: his death and resurrection. Help us not to chase dramatic signs, but to seek a deeper knowledge of you and your will. Give us hearts of repentance, so that we may respond to your call as the Ninevites and the Queen of the South did. May our lives prove our faith in you and our love for you. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and doesn’t find it.
Then he says, ‘I will return into my house from which I came out,’ and when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order.

Then he goes, and takes with himself seven other spirits more evil than he is, and they enter in and dwell there. The last state of that man becomes worse than the first. Even so will it be also to this evil generation.”
b: In this passage Jesus uses a parable about an unclean spirit to teach a deep spiritual truth. When an unclean spirit goes out of a person, it passes through dry places seeking rest but finds none, and decides to return to the house it left. When it arrives, it finds the house empty, swept and put in order, so it brings along seven other spirits more evil than itself and they enter and live there, and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first. Jesus tells this story to warn his hearers that merely getting rid of evil, without building a positive spiritual life in the heart, leads to a worse outcome.

Through this passage God reminds us that spiritual emptiness can lead to a worse spiritual state than before. When we drive sin and uncleanness out of our lives, we need to fill the space with the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. This passage urges us not only to cleanse our lives, but even more to cultivate positive spiritual qualities by staying continually close to Jesus Christ.
q: What “empty places” in my life might let the influence of sin and uncleanness come back in? How can I more actively seek to be filled with the Holy Spirit, so that these negative influences do not return?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for the teaching of Jesus Christ, which reminds us that cleansing the heart and filling the spirit are equally important. After we have driven sin and uncleanness out of our lives, help us fill our hearts with the fruit of the Spirit. Give us strength to grow in your love and truth, and to avoid spiritual emptiness and falling again. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: While he was yet speaking to the multitudes, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, seeking to speak to him.
One said to him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers stand outside, seeking to speak to you.”
But he answered him who spoke to him, “Who is my mother? Who are my brothers?”
He stretched out his hand toward his disciples, and said, “Behold, my mother and my brothers!
For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.”
b: In this passage, while Jesus is teaching the crowds, his mother and brothers come and stand outside, wanting to speak with him. When someone tells Jesus, he uses the occasion to explain the true meaning of the spiritual family. Jesus asks, “Who is my mother? Who are my brothers?” Then he points to his disciples and declares that those who do the will of his Father are his true family. This stresses that spiritual relationships go beyond biological ties of blood; they are based on shared faith and obedience to God's will.

This passage shows us that in Christ, spiritual family relationships are built on doing God's will. Jesus challenges the traditional view of family in his society, reminding us that true spiritual closeness comes from serving and loving God together. It teaches us that, as Christians, we should make doing God's will the deepest foundation that binds us to one another, a bond that reaches far beyond blood or cultural boundaries.
q: How do I understand and practice the idea of the spiritual family? In my church and daily life, do I truly regard those who do God's will as my family? How can I improve and deepen these spiritual relationships?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you that through your Son Jesus Christ we understand what a true spiritual family is. Help us to see more deeply that doing your will is the strongest bond that joins us. Give us loving hearts to welcome and care for the brothers and sisters who walk with us in faith. Help us grow in your love, and be bound more closely to you and to your people. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: On that day Jesus went out of the house, and sat by the seaside.
Great multitudes gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat, and sat, and all the multitude stood on the beach.
He spoke to them many things in parables, saying, “Behold, a farmer went out to sow.
As he sowed, some seeds fell by the roadside, and the birds came and devoured them.
Others fell on rocky ground, where they didn’t have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, because they had no depth of earth.
When the sun had risen, they were scorched. Because they had no root, they withered away.
Others fell among thorns. The thorns grew up and choked them.
Others fell on good soil, and yielded fruit: some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.
He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
The disciples came, and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?”
He answered them, “To you it is given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven, but it is not given to them.
For whoever has, to him will be given, and he will have abundance, but whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he has.
b: In this passage Jesus uses the parable of the sower to teach his hearers the truth about the kingdom of heaven. The seed in the parable stands for the word of God, and the different soils stand for the different ways people's hearts receive it. Seed on the path is exposed and eaten by birds; seed on rocky ground has no deep root and quickly withers; seed among thorns is choked with no room to grow; only seed on good soil bears abundant fruit. The parable reveals how differently people respond to the gospel, and stresses that a prepared heart can bear fruit abundantly.

Jesus used parables to teach the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven because parables reveal the depth of the hearers' hearts and how they respond to God's word. This passage not only describes how the gospel is received, but also reminds us that true understanding and growth come from receiving God's word deeply and honestly.

Through this passage God reminds us to examine how our hearts receive his word. He encourages us to be good soil, letting his word take deep root in our hearts, so that we may bear abundant spiritual fruit.
q: Is my heart truly open to receive the word of God? When I meet difficulties and temptations in life, how do I respond? What does the soil of my heart need, so that God's word can bear abundant fruit in it?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us through the parables of Jesus Christ. Help us be good soil, so that your word takes root and sprouts in our hearts and bears fruit a hundredfold. Lord, give us ears to hear and hearts to understand, so that we may fully receive and practice your word. We pray in Jesus' name. Amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they don’t see, and hearing, they don’t hear, neither do they understand.
In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled, which says, ‘By hearing you will hear, and will in no way understand; Seeing you will see, and will in no way perceive:

for this people’s heart has grown callous, their ears are dull of hearing, they have closed their eyes; or else perhaps they might perceive with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and would turn again; and I would heal them.’
“But blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your ears, for they hear.
For most certainly I tell you that many prophets and righteous men desired to see the things which you see, and didn’t see them; and to hear the things which you hear, and didn’t hear them.
b: In this passage Jesus explains why he teaches the crowds in parables. He points out that although people can see and hear physically, spiritually they neither see nor hear the truth, and this fulfills the prophecy of Isaiah. Jesus notes that the hearts of some have grown dull, and they are unwilling to turn and be healed. Yet he also stresses how blessed the disciples are, because they can understand and receive the truth of the kingdom of heaven, something that many prophets and righteous people longed to see but did not.

This passage speaks of the importance of spiritual perception and the challenges that come with it. Jesus teaches in parables because parables reveal the attitude of the hearers, and only those who are ready to receive and understand can truly grasp their meaning.

Through this passage God reminds us that true understanding is not merely hearing and seeing, but an awakening and change of heart. He calls us to open our hearts, and not let the busyness and temptations of the world keep us from hearing his voice. God also reminds us to treasure this opportunity to come into contact with his word and understand it, something that many prophets and righteous people hoped for but never received.
q: In my daily life, what things or attitudes may be keeping me from understanding and experiencing God's word more deeply? How can I overcome these obstacles, and open my heart more to God's teaching?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that through your Son Jesus Christ our eyes can see and our ears can hear your word. Help us open our hearts and not be blinded by the noise of the world, so that we can deeply understand and practice your teaching. Let our lives be transformed by your word, and draw us closer to you. We pray in the name of Jesus Christ. Amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Hear, then, the parable of the farmer.
When anyone hears the word of the Kingdom, and doesn’t understand it, the evil one comes, and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown by the roadside.
What was sown on the rocky places, this is he who hears the word, and immediately with joy receives it;
yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while. When oppression or persecution arises because of the word, immediately he stumbles.
What was sown among the thorns, this is he who hears the word, but the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful.
What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.”
b: This passage is Jesus' further explanation of the parable of the sower, making clear what the different responses to God's word mean. Jesus explains that the different soils stand for the different ways hearts receive the word of God. On the path, the seed is snatched away by the evil one; this pictures those who hear God's word but do not understand it. The rocky ground pictures those who receive the word with joy at first, but quickly fall away when trouble and persecution come. The thorny ground pictures those who are drawn away by worldly worries and wealth, so that God's word is choked and bears no fruit. Finally, the good soil pictures those who hear and understand God's word and let it bear abundant fruit.

This passage stresses how the way hearers receive God's word shapes the outcome of their lives. Through this parable Jesus teaches us that true faith is not only hearing God's word, but letting it take root in our hearts and putting it into practice in our lives.

Through this passage God reminds us that receiving his word requires a prepared heart and lasting commitment. We should receive his word not only when we feel good, but hold on to our faith in adversity. We must also be on guard against worldly temptations, and not let them suppress or take away our faith.
q: When I face challenges and temptations in life, how do I stay faithful and passionate toward God's word? What specific actions can I take to strengthen the faith in my heart, so that God's word takes deeper root in my life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for the teaching of Jesus Christ, which helps us understand how to receive and nurture your word. Help us be good soil, so that your word takes root and sprouts in our hearts, and bears abundant fruit in our lives. When trials and temptations come, give us strength and wisdom to stay on your path. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field,
but while people slept, his enemy came and sowed darnel weeds also among the wheat, and went away.
But when the blade sprang up and produced fruit, then the darnel weeds appeared also.
The servants of the householder came and said to him, ‘Sir, didn’t you sow good seed in your field? Where did these darnel weeds come from?’
“He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ “The servants asked him, ‘Do you want us to go and gather them up?’
“But he said, ‘No, lest perhaps while you gather up the darnel weeds, you root up the wheat with them.

Let both grow together until the harvest, and in the harvest time I will tell the reapers, “First, gather up the darnel weeds, and bind them in bundles to burn them; but gather the wheat into my barn.” ’ ”
b: In this passage Jesus uses a parable, known as the parable of the wheat and the weeds, to describe the kingdom of heaven. In the story, a man sows good seed in his field, but while everyone sleeps, his enemy comes and sows weeds among the wheat. When the wheat and the weeds grow up together, the servants discover the weeds and ask whether they should pull them up. The owner answers that there is no need to hurry, lest they uproot the wheat along with them; instead they should wait and separate them at harvest time.

This parable tells us that good and evil will exist together in the world until the final judgment. Jesus reminds us that the kingdom of heaven and the world are intertwined, and that we cannot decide for ourselves who is good and who is evil; that is something God will ultimately decide.

This passage reminds us that in our lives we will meet all kinds of people and situations, a mixture of good and evil. God wants us to be patient and tolerant, not hasty to judge or to remove what seems bad, because the final judgment belongs to God alone. It also teaches us to trust God's wisdom and justice, even when, on the surface, things look confusing and unclear.
q: How do I handle the injustice or wrongdoing I meet in life? Am I too quick to judge or to act? How can I better reflect God's patience and tolerance?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for the parable of Jesus Christ, which teaches us patience and tolerance in a world where good and evil exist together. Give us wisdom and discernment to wait for your judgment in your own time. Help us not to act hastily, but to rely on your justice and fairness. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field;
which indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs, and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches.”
He spoke another parable to them. “The Kingdom of Heaven is like yeast, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, until it was all leavened.”
Jesus spoke all these things in parables to the multitudes; and without a parable, he didn’t speak to them,
that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet, saying, “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.”
b: In these verses Jesus reveals the nature of the kingdom of heaven through two parables, the mustard seed and the leaven. Together they stress that the kingdom of heaven begins small and ends by growing into a large and far-reaching influence.

The parable of the mustard seed says that the kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, the smallest of all seeds, which when planted grows into a tree, so large that birds come and nest in its branches. This parable reveals that although the kingdom of heaven begins small, its potential for growth is great, and in the end it can provide shelter and rest.

The parable of the leaven describes a woman who hides a little yeast in a large amount of flour until the whole batch is leavened. This teaches us that the kingdom of heaven is like a little leaven that can affect and change the whole structure, even if it starts out unnoticed.
Through these parables Jesus tells us that the work of the kingdom of heaven begins in small ways, quietly influencing everything around it, and in the end reaches remarkable results.

Through this passage God reminds us not to despise what seem to be insignificant beginnings. Whether it is our faith or the small seeds in our actions, each has the potential to grow into something with wide influence. God encourages us to have patience and foresight, and to believe that he can bring great change through our lives and actions.
q: What seemingly small actions in my life might have a positive influence on others or on society? How can I more consciously nurture these “mustard seeds,” so that they grow and extend their influence?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you for teaching us, through the parables of Jesus Christ, the wonder and power of the kingdom of heaven. Give us faith to believe that even the smallest beginning can bring great change. Help us see the importance of every small act, and live out your kingdom in our daily lives. We ask you to guide us, so that we may become instruments of your grace and love. We pray in Jesus' name. Amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Then Jesus sent the multitudes away, and went into the house. His disciples came to him, saying, “Explain to us the parable of the darnel weeds of the field.”
He answered them, “He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man,
the field is the world; and the good seed, these are the children of the Kingdom; and the darnel weeds are the children of the evil one.
The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.
As therefore the darnel weeds are gathered up and burned with fire; so will it be at the end of this age.
The Son of Man will send out his angels, and they will gather out of his Kingdom all things that cause stumbling, and those who do iniquity,
and will cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be the weeping and the gnashing of teeth.
Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the Kingdom of their Father. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.
b: In this passage Jesus explains to His disciples the parable of the weeds in the field that He had told earlier. He says plainly that the good seed represents "the sons of the Kingdom," while the weeds represent "the sons of the evil one." Jesus Himself is the Son of Man who sows the good seed, and the field is the world. The enemy who sows the weeds is the devil, the harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.

The passage shows that good and evil will be clearly separated at the end of the age. The sons of the evil one will be gathered out and thrown into the furnace of fire, while the sons of the Kingdom will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom. Through this parable Jesus stresses the final fulfillment of righteousness, the ultimate victory of the righteous, and the downfall of the evil one.

Through this passage God reminds us that although good and evil are hard to separate completely in the present world, a day of final judgment is coming. This teaches us to hold on with faith and patience, trusting that God will bring justice in His own time. It also encourages us, as sons of the Kingdom, to shine in the world and to hold fast to our faith until the end.
q: In my daily life, how do I show that I am a child of the Kingdom? When I face moral and ethical challenges, how do I keep my conduct pure and upright?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, we thank You for explaining the mysteries of the Kingdom to us through Your Son, Jesus Christ. Give us firm faith, so that even in hardship and trials we may hold on to our belief, knowing that You will bring justice at last and give the righteous glory at the end of the age. Help us walk in Your light and become lights in the world. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you!

v: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like treasure hidden in the field, which a man found, and hid. In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has, and buys that field.
“Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who is a merchant seeking fine pearls,
who having found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
“Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a dragnet, that was cast into the sea, and gathered some fish of every kind,
which, when it was filled, they drew up on the beach. They sat down, and gathered the good into containers, but the bad they threw away.
So will it be in the end of the world. The angels will come and separate the wicked from among the righteous,
and will cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be the weeping and the gnashing of teeth.”
Jesus said to them, “Have you understood all these things?” They answered him, “Yes, Lord.”
He said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been made a disciple in the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who is a householder, who brings out of his treasure new and old things.”
When Jesus had finished these parables, he departed from there.
b: In this passage Jesus uses three parables to portray the preciousness of the Kingdom of Heaven and the final judgment. First, the Kingdom is like a treasure hidden in a field; the one who finds it gives up everything to obtain it. Next, the Kingdom is like a pearl of great price; the merchant likewise sells all that he has in order to own it. These two parables stress the supreme worth of the Kingdom and the wholehearted devotion and sacrifice that seeking it requires.

The third parable compares the Kingdom to a net cast into the sea that gathers fish of every kind; in the end the good are kept and the bad are thrown away. This pictures the judgment at the end of the age, when the angels will separate the righteous from the wicked.

Through these parables Jesus stresses that the value of the Kingdom far exceeds everything we own, and that it is worth giving all we have to pursue it. They also remind us that a day will come when everything is judged and good and evil are clearly divided.

Through this passage God calls us to recognize how important it is to seek the Kingdom, and to give everything for it. He encourages us to treasure spiritual things above worldly wealth and to prepare for the day of final judgment. It is a life-shaping choice: to pursue what is eternal rather than the passing satisfactions of the moment.
q: In my pursuit of the Kingdom, what do I need to give up or sacrifice? How can I invest my time, energy, and resources more effectively in the values of the Kingdom, so that I will be approved by the Lord at the end of the age?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for revealing the mystery and worth of the Kingdom through the teaching of Jesus Christ. Help us seek the treasure of heaven with all our hearts and be willing to give up everything to gain it. When the day of judgment comes, may we be counted among Your righteous ones. Give us wisdom and strength to persevere to the end and to glorify Your name. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you!

v: Coming into his own country, he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom, and these mighty works?
Isn’t this the carpenter’s son? Isn’t his mother called Mary, and his brothers, James, Joses, Simon, and Judas?
Aren’t all of his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all of these things?”
They were offended by him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor, except in his own country, and in his own house.”
He didn’t do many mighty works there because of their unbelief.
b: In this passage Jesus returns to His hometown of Nazareth and teaches in the synagogue. The people are amazed at His wisdom and miracles, but they are also troubled by His family background and begin to question where His power comes from. Because they know His family and origins so well, they cannot accept Him as a prophet. Jesus says that a prophet is honored everywhere except in his own hometown and his own household. Because of their unbelief, He did not do many mighty works there.

This passage reveals how prejudice toward what is familiar can block the reception of truth. The people of His hometown could not accept anything beyond the fixed idea they had of who He was, and this finally limited their chance to experience the miraculous.

Through this passage God reminds us not to let prejudice and preconceived ideas keep us from receiving the gifts and abilities that God gives through others. We should keep an open heart and recognize that God can work through anyone, whatever their background. We should learn to respect and welcome what God does, even when it comes from an unexpected place.
q: In my own life, have I overlooked a way God might be speaking to me through someone because I was too familiar with them or the situation? How can I grow in receiving and respecting people from different backgrounds?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for reminding us, through what Jesus experienced in Nazareth, not to let prejudice and familiarity keep us from seeing Your work. Help us keep an open heart, ready to receive miracles and teaching from unexpected places. Give us humble hearts, so that in every circumstance we may see Your grace and power. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you!

v: At that time, Herod the tetrarch heard the report concerning Jesus,
and said to his servants, “This is John the Baptizer. He is risen from the dead. That is why these powers work in him.”
For Herod had arrested John, and bound him, and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife.
For John said to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.”
When he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet.
But when Herod’s birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced among them and pleased Herod.
Whereupon he promised with an oath to give her whatever she should ask.
She, being prompted by her mother, said, “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptizer.”
The king was grieved, but for the sake of his oaths, and of those who sat at the table with him, he commanded it to be given,
and he sent and beheaded John in the prison.
His head was brought on a platter, and given to the young lady; and she brought it to her mother.
His disciples came, and took the body, and buried it. Then they went and told Jesus.
Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat, to a deserted place apart. When the multitudes heard it, they followed him on foot from the cities.
b: Matthew 14 describes the tragic end of John the Baptist and Jesus' response to the news. Out of fear of the people and because of his own oath, King Herod was forced to have John beheaded, granting the demand of Herodias' daughter and her mother. The passage shows not only Herod's moral struggle and final surrender, but also how politics and personal desire can combine to produce injustice. When Jesus heard of John's death, He withdrew alone to a desolate place to mourn, showing His respect for John and His grief.

This passage shows us that even in extreme adversity the voice of justice and truth must not be silenced. John spoke up fearlessly for the truth, even though it finally cost him his life. It teaches us to stand courageously on the side of justice, even in the face of severe consequences. Jesus' response also reminds us that when we face loss and grief, seeking solitude with God is a way to recover strength and peace.
q: How do I respond to situations that threaten my honesty and integrity? Do I sometimes compromise my principles to avoid conflict or consequences? Under the pressures and challenges of life, how can I find time alone with God and receive strength and guidance from Him?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, in the story of John we see the power of justice and truth, and we also witness the challenges they face. Grant us courage and wisdom, so that in every situation we may stand firm for what is right and not fear any threat or temptation. When we meet loss and grief, let us find moments of restoration and peace in Your presence. Help us follow Jesus, with a humble heart that seeks Your will. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Jesus went out, and he saw a great multitude. He had compassion on them, and healed their sick.

When evening had come, his disciples came to him, saying, “This place is deserted, and the hour is already late. Send the multitudes away, that they may go into the villages, and buy themselves food.”
But Jesus said to them, “They don’t need to go away. You give them something to eat.”
They told him, “We only have here five loaves and two fish.”
He said, “Bring them here to me.”

He commanded the multitudes to sit down on the grass; and he took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, broke and gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples gave to the multitudes.
They all ate, and were filled. They took up twelve baskets full of that which remained left over from the broken pieces.
Those who ate were about five thousand men, in addition to women and children.
b: This passage describes the miracle of Jesus feeding five thousand people in a desolate place. When Jesus saw the great crowd that followed Him, He was moved by their need and healed their sick. That evening the disciples suggested sending the crowds away to buy food in the nearby villages. Jesus instead chose to work a miracle with five loaves and two fish, and fed everyone. The story shows not only Jesus' concern for people's physical and spiritual needs, but also His supernatural power.

Through this miracle Jesus teaches us to trust in God's provision. Even when our resources seem too small to meet the need, God's power can take us beyond material limits. The passage reminds us that when we offer to God all that we have, even if it is insignificant, He can use it in wonderful ways to meet the needs of many. It challenges our faith and our actions, and encourages us to trust God even when a situation looks impossible.
q: In which areas of my life do I need to trust God's provision more? Am I holding back some resources from God because I fear they won't be enough? How can I practice the principle of offering my "five loaves and two fish" to God in daily life?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, we thank You for the abundant provision and wonderful works You have shown in our lives. Help us grow in confidence in Your limitless resources, and trust You even when things seem impossible. Make us instruments of Your generous giving, that we may bless others with what we hold in our hands. In our lives, let us witness Your love and great power, and let us be bold to act and give when there is need. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat, and to go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the multitudes away.
After he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into the mountain by himself to pray. When evening had come, he was there alone.
But the boat was now in the middle of the sea, distressed by the waves, for the wind was contrary.
In the fourth watch of the night, Jesus came to them, walking on the sea.
When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, “It’s a ghost!” and they cried out for fear.
But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Cheer up! It is I!  Don’t be afraid.”
Peter answered him and said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.”
He said, “Come!” Peter stepped down from the boat, and walked on the waters to come to Jesus.
But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, “Lord, save me!”
Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”
When they got up into the boat, the wind ceased.
Those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying, “You are truly the Son of God!”
When they had crossed over, they came to the land of Gennesaret.
When the people of that place recognized him, they sent into all that surrounding region, and brought to him all who were sick;
and they begged him that they might just touch the fringe of his garment. As many as touched it were made whole.
b: This passage describes the miracle of Jesus walking on the sea, and Peter's attempt to walk on the water. After sending the disciples across the sea, Jesus went up the mountain alone to pray. When the boat was battered by wind and waves, Jesus came to them in the night, walking on the sea, and the disciples were at first terrified. Peter, in faith, asked to come to Jesus on the water, but when he noticed the strong wind he began to sink and cried out for help. Jesus immediately reached out His hand and rebuked him for his little faith. When they got into the boat, the wind ceased, and those in the boat gained a deeper knowledge of Jesus' deity and worshiped Him. At the end of the passage, Jesus and the disciples land at Gennesaret, where the crowds welcome Him eagerly and seek His healing.

This passage reminds us of Jesus' care for us and of His supernatural power. When the disciples faced difficulty and fear, Jesus not only came to them Himself, but also comforted and encouraged them. He allowed Peter to experience the power of stepping out in faith, and also showed the consequences of insufficient faith. This teaches us that when we face the storms of life, we should fix our eyes on Jesus and depend on His strength rather than on our feelings or circumstances.
q: What "storms" in my life are testing my faith? How am I responding to these challenges? How can I more effectively turn my focus from my difficulties to Jesus, and so be strengthened in faith and find peace?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us, through Your Son Jesus Christ, Your limitless power and Your deep care for us. Help us stand firm in faith through difficulties and trials, focusing on You rather than on our fears. When we go through storms, let us remember that You are always with us, and that Your strength is enough to carry us over every challenge. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem, saying,
“Why do your disciples disobey the tradition of the elders? For they don’t wash their hands when they eat bread.”
He answered them, “Why do you also disobey the commandment of God because of your tradition?
For God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him be put to death.’
But you say, ‘Whoever may tell his father or his mother, “Whatever help you might otherwise have gotten from me is a gift devoted to God,”
he shall not honor his father or mother.’ You have made the commandment of God void because of your tradition.
You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, saying,
‘These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.
And in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrine rules made by men.’ ”
b: In this passage Jesus argues with the Pharisees and scribes over the traditional rule of washing hands. When asked why His disciples do not keep the tradition of the elders, Jesus asks in return why they let man-made rules override the commandment of God. He points out their hypocrisy: they honor God outwardly, yet place human teaching above God's commandments. The passage exposes the emptiness of outward formalism and stresses that a true inner relationship with God matters far more than outward religious ritual.

Through this passage God reminds us that true worship is not outward observance of rituals or traditions, but the sincere engagement of the heart and spirit. Jesus criticizes those who keep religious rules on the surface while their hearts are far from God. This reminds us to examine whether our practice of faith truly honors God. God wants our hearts, not merely outward obedience.
q: What outward religious activities in my life may have replaced sincere worship of God? How can I turn my heart to God more truly, and not be content with religious formality?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your word what true worship is. Help us not to seek merely outward conformity to religious norms, but to worship and serve You with sincere hearts in our everyday lives. Search our hearts, and remove all hypocrisy and pride from among us, so that with pure hearts we may honor Your commandments. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He summoned the multitude, and said to them, “Hear, and understand.
That which enters into the mouth doesn’t defile the man; but that which proceeds out of the mouth, this defiles the man.”
Then the disciples came, and said to him, “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?”
But he answered, “Every plant which my heavenly Father didn’t plant will be uprooted.
Leave them alone. They are blind guides of the blind. If the blind guide the blind, both will fall into a pit.”
Peter answered him, “Explain the parable to us.”
So Jesus said, “Do you also still not understand?
Don’t you understand that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the belly, and then out of the body?
But the things which proceed out of the mouth come out of the heart, and they defile the man.
For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual sins, thefts, false testimony, and blasphemies.
These are the things which defile the man; but to eat with unwashed hands doesn’t defile the man.”
Jesus went out from there, and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon.
b: In this passage Jesus teaches the crowd and His disciples about what truly defiles a person. He points out that what defiles is not something outside, like the food that goes into the mouth, but the evil thoughts and deeds that come out of the heart. Jesus rebukes the religious leaders of the day for stressing ritual cleanness too much, and emphasizes that purity of heart matters more than keeping outward traditions. It is a direct response to the Pharisees, whose righteousness was on the surface and whose conduct was hypocritical.

This passage reminds us that true purity works from the inside out, and is more than keeping outward rules. God looks at our hearts and at the words and actions that flow from them. Our life of faith should reflect a deep love for God and a sincere keeping of His commands. This challenges us to examine our attitudes and behavior, and to ask whether they truly reflect the love and reverence for God within us.
q: Looking back over the past week, which of my actions came from social or religious expectations rather than from sincere love for God? How can I focus more on cultivating a clean heart and truly do God's will?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your word that true purity begins in the heart. Help us stay alert and not be deceived by outward religious behavior, but keep our hearts spotless before You. Help us so that all we think and do in daily life may glorify You and show Your work in our lives. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those borders, and cried, saying, “Have mercy on me, Lord, you son of David! My daughter is severely possessed by a demon!”
But he answered her not a word. His disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away; for she cries after us.”
But he answered, “I wasn’t sent to anyone but the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”
But she came and worshiped him, saying, “Lord, help me.”
But he answered, “It is not appropriate to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”
But she said, “Yes, Lord, but even the dogs eat the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.”
Then Jesus answered her, “Woman, great is your faith! Be it done to you even as you desire.” And her daughter was healed from that hour.
b: This passage records the story of a Canaanite woman who came to Jesus asking for healing for her demon-possessed daughter. Jesus' initial silence and the response that followed seem cold, but they were in fact a test of the woman's faith. Jesus calls the people of Israel "children," implying that He was sent first to Israel; to give the children's bread (blessing) to the "dogs" (Gentiles) seemed not right. Yet the woman's answer shows her humility and firm faith: she accepts her place, but still persists in asking for help.

Jesus' praise for this woman, "Woman, great is your faith!", shows the importance of faith, even in seemingly impossible situations. Jesus not only healed her daughter, but also showed that God's grace goes far beyond the borders of Israel and is open to all peoples.

Through this passage God reminds us that true faith is not limited to one people or tradition; it is about firmly trusting God's power and love. This teaches us that even in despair we should keep seeking God and believe in His good plan for our lives.
q: Think back: have I sometimes lacked faith in difficult times? How can I put a deeper trust in and reliance on God into practice in daily life?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us Your boundless love and mercy through Jesus Christ. Strengthen our faith, so that when we face hardship we may keep seeking Your help, believing that You will show grace and blessing according to our needs. Help us learn the unyielding faith of the Canaanite woman, and put our trust in You into practice in our lives. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you!

v: Jesus departed from there, and came near to the sea of Galilee; and he went up into the mountain, and sat there.
Great multitudes came to him, having with them the lame, blind, mute, maimed, and many others, and they put them down at his feet. He healed them,
so that the multitude wondered when they saw the mute speaking, the injured healed, the lame walking, and the blind seeing—and they glorified the God of Israel.

Jesus summoned his disciples and said, “I have compassion on the multitude, because they continue with me now three days and have nothing to eat. I don’t want to send them away fasting, or they might faint on the way.”
The disciples said to him, “Where should we get so many loaves in a deserted place as to satisfy so great a multitude?”
Jesus said to them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven, and a few small fish.”
He commanded the multitude to sit down on the ground;
and he took the seven loaves and the fish. He gave thanks and broke them, and gave to the disciples, and the disciples to the multitudes.
They all ate, and were filled. They took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces that were left over.
Those who ate were four thousand men, in addition to women and children.
Then he sent away the multitudes, got into the boat, and came into the borders of Magdala.
b: This passage describes Jesus performing a series of wonderful healings on a mountain beside the Sea of Galilee, and showing His compassion and power through miracles. Jesus not only healed the lame, the blind, the mute, and many others who were sick, but also provided materially for the crowd, feeding four thousand. In this passage Jesus twice speaks of His compassion for the crowd, shown not only in His acts of healing but also in His concern for their physical hunger.

Through these actions Jesus shows us God's comprehensive care for human need, both physical and spiritual. He teaches us that true service is whole-hearted: not only the salvation of souls, but also care for people's practical needs. Through His deeds Jesus confirms that love and service toward the least and weakest are at the heart of the Kingdom of God.

In addition, Jesus fed the multitude with limited resources, seven loaves and a few small fish. This shows His creative provision, and also symbolizes how God works in our lives in unexpected ways, creating abundance even when resources are scarce.
q: Looking back over my life, when have I experienced God's wonderful provision, material or spiritual? In future service, how can I respond more effectively to the needs of those around me?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us Your boundless compassion and almighty power through Jesus Christ. Help us follow Jesus, caring not only for the salvation of souls but also for people's daily needs. When we face situations that seem insufficient, let us remember that You can make the limited unlimited. Inspire us to love and to serve, as Jesus showed us. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you!

v: The Pharisees and Sadducees came, and testing him, asked him to show them a sign from heaven.
But he answered them, “When it is evening, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.’
In the morning, ‘It will be foul weather today, for the sky is red and threatening.’ Hypocrites! You know how to discern the appearance of the sky, but you can’t discern the signs of the times!
An evil and adulterous generation seeks after a sign, and there will be no sign given to it, except the sign of the prophet Jonah.” He left them, and departed.
b: In this passage the Pharisees and Sadducees come to test Jesus, demanding that He show them a sign from heaven. Their request does not come from a sincere search for faith, but from doubt and a challenge to Jesus' authority. Jesus' answer reveals His insight into their attitude: people can read the signs of nature, yet are blind to spiritual truth. Jesus rebukes their sign-seeking, saying that an evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and that the only sign given will be the sign of Jonah, which points ahead to Jesus' own resurrection from the dead.

This passage shows us that God expects us to follow Him by faith, not by a faith that demands miracles. It challenges us to reflect on our motives for seeking God: is it true faith, or a wish to see miracles that prove Him? Jesus' response reminds us that true faith should not depend on outward evidence, but be based on trust in God's word and on knowing His deity.
q: Think back: have I ever doubted God's work in my life because I saw no obvious miracle? How can I cultivate a heart that holds on to faith even when no miracles are seen?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us the true meaning of faith through Your Son Jesus Christ. Help us not merely to seek signs, but to understand and believe Your word more deeply. When we face doubts and temptations, strengthen our faith, and let our lives bear witness to Your glory. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you!

v: The disciples came to the other side and had forgotten to take bread.
Jesus said to them, “Take heed and beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”
They reasoned among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread.”
Jesus, perceiving it, said, “Why do you reason among yourselves, you of little faith, ‘because you have brought no bread?’
Don’t you yet perceive, neither remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you took up?
Nor the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you took up?
How is it that you don’t perceive that I didn’t speak to you concerning bread? But beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”
Then they understood that he didn’t tell them to beware of the yeast of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
b: In this passage Jesus takes the disciples' worry about physical bread and uses it to teach them a deep spiritual truth. When the disciples worry because they forgot to bring bread, Jesus tells them to pay more attention to "the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees." Here "leaven" symbolizes the teaching and attitude of faith of these religious leaders, which, like yeast, can influence and change the thinking and behavior of a whole group of people.

Jesus uses two miracles, the feeding of the five thousand with five loaves and two fish and of the four thousand with seven loaves, to remind the disciples of His provision, so that they need not worry about a shortage of material things. Jesus stresses that their focus should not be only on physical bread, but on discerning and resisting the false teaching that could corrupt their faith.

Through this passage God reminds us that spiritual alertness and discernment are abilities every believer must cultivate. We need to recognize the "leaven" in our lives, those subtle ideas and teachings that can fundamentally change our faith and behavior. Jesus' teaching is not only a reminder to the disciples of that day, but also a call to the church today, reminding us not to be influenced by the thinking of the world and by false notions of faith.
q: Think back: what "leaven" in my life may be quietly influencing my view of faith? How can I strengthen my discernment in faith, so as not to be misled by false teaching?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for reminding us through Your word that what matters most is not only material provision but spiritual awakening and insight. Help us recognize and avoid the teachings and ideas that, like leaven, can quietly influence our hearts. Give us wisdom, so that we may live out Your truth every day. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you!

v: Now when Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying, “Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?”
They said, “Some say John the Baptizer, some, Elijah, and others, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.”
He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?”
Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.
I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock  I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
I will give to you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven; and whatever you release on earth will have been released in heaven.”
b: In this passage Jesus asks His disciples a key question: "Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?" The question first reveals the different views people held about Jesus at that time: some thought He was one of the prophets, such as John, Elijah, or Jeremiah. But when Jesus turned the question directly to the disciples, and especially to Peter, Peter's answer showed deeper spiritual insight: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." This declaration not only affirms Jesus' deity, but also shows Peter's knowledge of Jesus' true identity, a knowledge revealed by the Father and not reached by human wisdom.

Jesus tells Peter he is blessed, because his knowledge came from revelation from heaven, which stresses that the revelation of spiritual truth goes beyond human understanding. Jesus then declares that He will build His church on this "rock," which refers to Peter's confession, that Jesus is the Son of God; this is the foundation of the church. Jesus also gives Peter the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven, which symbolize the ability to exercise heavenly authority in the church: whatever is bound or loosed on earth will be bound or loosed in heaven.

Through this passage God reminds us that knowing Jesus' true identity is the cornerstone of every believer. Our faith is built on knowing that He is the Christ, the Son of the living God. It also challenges us to reflect on whether our faith, like Peter's, is based on revelation from the Father, and whether we exercise heavenly authority in our lives.
q: Reflect: what is my personal answer to Jesus' question, "Who do you say that I am?" How does this knowledge affect my life of faith and my obedience to His commands?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for revealing Your truth to us through Jesus Christ. Help us stand firmly on the rock of knowing that Jesus is the Christ, and show this truth in our lives and service. Give us wisdom and strength to exercise effectively in the world the spiritual authority You have given. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you!

v: Then he commanded the disciples that they should tell no one that he was Jesus the Christ.
From that time, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised up.
Peter took him aside, and began to rebuke him, saying, “Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you.”
But he turned, and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.”
b: In this passage Jesus for the first time plainly tells His disciples about His coming suffering, death, and resurrection. His prophecy is not only about His own fate, but is a key part of God's plan of redemption. This revelation provokes a strong reaction from Peter, who is unwilling to accept that such an end could come to the Lord he loves and respects. His reaction comes from love and a desire to protect Jesus, but Jesus sternly corrects him, pointing out that at that moment Peter's thinking came from a human point of view, not God's.

Jesus says to Peter, "Get behind me, Satan." "Satan" means "adversary," and is another name for the devil. Jesus' command to step aside shows that Peter's thought at that moment was contrary to God's will and came from Satan's way of thinking. Jesus did this to teach Peter and the other disciples that they must go beyond human emotion and understanding to accept God's higher will and plan, and must not use human ideas to oppose God's. Jesus' road is the road of suffering that leads to the cross, an indispensable part of God's plan of redemption, so that the sins of all humanity might be forgiven and redeemed.

What God shows us through this passage is that the path of faith is sometimes full of sacrifice and commands that are hard to understand. As followers, we are called to lay down our own ideas and be willing to accept and obey God's plan, even when it seems full of pain and challenge.
q: Think about it: when in my life have I been like Peter, meaning well but actually hindering God's will? How can I learn to lay down my own will so as to follow God's plan better?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for revealing Your plan of redemption to us through Jesus Christ. Give us humble and obedient hearts, so that we can accept and follow Your plan, which is higher than our understanding. When we face difficulties and moments we do not understand, strengthen our faith, so that we may follow You without wavering. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you!

v: Then Jesus said to his disciples, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.
For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it.
For what will it profit a man, if he gains the whole world, and forfeits his life? Or what will a man give in exchange for his life?
For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will render to everyone according to his deeds.
Most certainly I tell you, there are some standing here who will in no way taste of death, until they see the Son of Man coming in his Kingdom.”
b: In this passage Jesus teaches His disciples and all who follow Him that following Him demands great personal sacrifice. When Jesus speaks of "denying self" and "taking up his cross," these acts symbolize complete self-denial and absolute obedience to God's will. This is a challenging road. It asks followers to give up not only material possessions but also the inner self and pride.

Jesus goes on to explain that those who refuse to follow Him in order to protect their own interests will lose their lives in a deeper sense. On the other hand, those who sacrifice themselves for Jesus and the gospel will find true life. Here "life" refers not only to existence in this world but also to eternal life and salvation.

Jesus' words reach a climax as He speaks of His coming again and the final judgment. This stresses that everyone's deeds will be examined, and each will be repaid according to what they have done on earth. It is a strong reminder that spiritual pursuits are far more important than worldly gain.

Through this passage God reminds us that following Jesus means making a true self-sacrifice, letting go of the attractions of the world, and focusing on spiritual growth and eternal values. He encourages us to reflect on our priorities and the direction of our lives, so that we may live out God's calling more fully.
q: In my life, what concrete ways can help me to better "deny myself" and "take up my cross"? How can I express in practice my following of Christ and my perseverance in faith?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for the teaching of Your Son Jesus Christ, reminding us that following You means denying self and bearing the cross. Give us strength and courage, so that we may let go of everything that hinders us from walking with You. Help us measure everything by the values of the Kingdom of Heaven, and seek true life in Your glorious kingdom. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you!

v: After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves.
He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light.
Behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them talking with him.
Peter answered, and said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”
While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.”
When the disciples heard it, they fell on their faces, and were very afraid.
Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.”
Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.
b: This passage records the transfiguration of Jesus, a remarkable moment in which He reveals His divine glory. Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain and is transfigured before them. In this extraordinary scene His face shines like the sun and His clothes become white as light, showing His divine nature and authority, which surpass those of ordinary people.

Even more remarkable is the appearance of Moses and Elijah, the most important figures of the Old Testament, representing the Law and the Prophets. Their conversation with Jesus symbolizes that the Law and the Prophets both bear witness to Jesus. Peter's reaction shows that he did not fully grasp the importance of the event: he proposes to build three tents, one for Jesus, one for Moses, and one for Elijah, which shows that he did not yet fully understand Jesus' unique position.

God speaks from the cloud, declaring that Jesus is His beloved Son, in whom He is well pleased, and commands the disciples to listen to Him. This is divine affirmation of Jesus' identity and mission, and direct guidance for the disciples, stressing that Jesus is greater than the Law and the Prophets of the Old Testament and is the center of the new era.

What God shows us through this passage is that Jesus is the pinnacle of God's revelation. He is our final authority, and we should listen to His teaching and follow in His footsteps. Jesus is not only a teacher or prophet in history; He is the Lord of life, the beloved Son of God, and the center of our faith and life.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you!

v: As they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying, “Don’t tell anyone what you saw, until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.”
His disciples asked him, saying, “Then why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”
Jesus answered them, “Elijah indeed comes first, and will restore all things,
but I tell you that Elijah has come already, and they didn’t recognize him, but did to him whatever they wanted to. Even so the Son of Man will also suffer by them.”
Then the disciples understood that he spoke to them of John the Baptizer.
b: This passage describes the conversation between Jesus and the three disciples as they come down the mountain. Jesus orders them not to tell anyone what they had seen on the mountain until the Son of Man has risen from the dead. This shows Jesus' clear understanding of His own mission and the timing of His plan.

When the disciples ask about the prophecy that Elijah must come first, Jesus explains that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but "did to him whatever they pleased." Here Jesus is speaking of John the Baptist, who, in the role of Elijah, came to fulfill God's mission but was ignored and mistreated. This reminds the disciples that Jesus Himself will face a similar fate.

This passage teaches us that even when God's prophets and messengers appear, people may still fail to recognize them and accept their message. Jesus stresses that truly knowing God's will requires going beyond surface views and expectations.

Through this passage God reminds us that recognizing God's work and plan sometimes requires us to go beyond traditional ideas and preconceived expectations. Jesus' words challenge us to remain faithful and obedient even when things are difficult or misunderstood.
q: When I meet situations that seem to contradict God's will, how do I seek and confirm God's guidance?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for teaching us through Your word to know Your plan and will. Help us, like Jesus and John the Baptist, to keep delivering Your message even in adversity. Let our faith be built not only on the miracles we see, but on a deep knowledge and experience of You. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When they came to the multitude, a man came to him, kneeling down to him, and saying,
“Lord, have mercy on my son, for he is epileptic, and suffers grievously; for he often falls into the fire, and often into the water.
So I brought him to your disciples, and they could not cure him.”
Jesus answered, “Faithless and perverse generation! How long will I be with you? How long will I bear with you? Bring him here to me.”
Jesus rebuked him, the demon went out of him, and the boy was cured from that hour.
Then the disciples came to Jesus privately, and said, “Why weren’t we able to cast it out?”

He said to them, “Because of your unbelief. For most certainly I tell you, if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will tell this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you.
But this kind doesn’t go out except by prayer and fasting.”
b: This passage tells of a father who seeks Jesus' help for his epileptic son. At the time, epilepsy was thought to be demon possession. The father first sought help from the disciples, but they could not heal the boy. Jesus' response then reveals His disappointment at the little faith of the believers of that time, and He calls them to strengthen their faith.

Jesus' response stresses the power of faith and the importance of prayer and fasting in spiritual warfare. When Jesus rebuked the demon, the boy was healed at once, showing His supreme authority and rule over the spiritual realm. Jesus then explained to the disciples that casting out this kind of demon requires greater faith, strengthened through prayer and fasting.

This teaches us that some spiritual challenges require extraordinary spiritual discipline to overcome. Jesus stresses that even faith as small as a mustard seed can do great things. This is not only a reminder to the disciples of that time, but also an encouragement to all believers, telling us to rely on God's power when we face difficulties and challenges.
q: In which areas of my life do I need to strengthen faith and spiritual discipline to face the challenge? How do I practice prayer and fasting to seek God's help?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for the authority and power You have shown us through Your Son Jesus Christ. Help us, when we face challenges in life, not to rely on our own strength, but on the faith You give, and to seek Your help and guidance through prayer and fasting. Increase our faith, so that we can do greater works for You in Your Kingdom. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: While they were staying in Galilee, Jesus said to them, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered up into the hands of men,
and they will kill him, and the third day he will be raised up.” They were exceedingly sorry.
When they had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma coins came to Peter, and said, “Doesn’t your teacher pay the didrachma?”

He said, “Yes.” When he came into the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying, “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive toll or tribute? From their children, or from strangers?”
Peter said to him, “From strangers.” Jesus said to him, “Therefore the children are exempt.

But, lest we cause them to stumble, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take up the first fish that comes up. When you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater coin. Take that, and give it to them for me and you.”
b: In this passage Jesus once again foretells His suffering and resurrection. He tells the disciples plainly that He will be delivered into the hands of men and killed, but on the third day will be raised. This prophecy fills the disciples with deep sorrow and confusion, because they cannot yet fully understand the meaning and necessity of these things.

The passage then turns to a conversation between Jesus and Peter about the temple tax. When asked whether He pays the tax, Jesus uses the opportunity to teach Peter about the privilege of the citizens of the Kingdom: the sons of God are free from the tax. Yet, so as not to give a bad impression or cause needless offense, Jesus tells Peter to go fishing and to find in the mouth of the first fish he catches enough money to pay the tax for both of them. This miracle shows not only Jesus' command over nature, but also His sensitivity to social responsibility.

Through this passage God reveals to us the foretelling of Christ's suffering and His care for the disciples. Jesus cares not only about spiritual teaching but also about practical matters of daily life. He teaches us to attend to the things of the Kingdom, and also to handle worldly obligations well, avoiding needless conflict.
q: When have I needed to find a balance between keeping my principles of faith and meeting social responsibilities? How can I take an active part in society as a Christian without compromising my faith?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You for showing us through Jesus Christ how to balance our spiritual calling with the responsibilities of daily life. Give us wisdom, so that while following Your will we may also set an example in society and fulfill the duties we owe. When we face difficulties and temptations, give us faith and strength, believing that You will prepare the way for us. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: In that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying, “Who then is greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven?”
